title: Ridge Runner
summary: Plant a flag at a hilltop, a valley floor or the highest point of a walk using f′, the sign change and the second derivative test.
subject: mathematics
concepts: Points that are not extrema (flat spots)
Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
learningOutcome: The student can find the critical points of a function, say whether each is a maximum, a minimum or neither, and find the absolute extremes on a closed interval including its end points.

levels.title: Hilltop or valley
levels.adds: Baseline: find f′ = 0, then use f″ (negative for a hilltop, positive for a valley) or the sign change (Ex 6.3 Q3, Q4; Examples 17 to 21).
hints: Differentiate and set f′(x) = 0; the roots are the candidates.
Check f″ at each root: negative means the ground bends down, a hilltop.
Or check the sign of f′ just before and just after.

levels.title: The flat spot trap
levels.adds: New: a squared factor in f′ gives a zero where the sign does not change, so it is neither a peak nor a valley (Examples 19, 21; Misc Q10).
hints: Find every zero of f′, then look at the sign of f′ on both sides of each.
A factor like (x − a)² never changes sign, so a is a flat spot.
The turning point is where the sign really changes.

levels.title: Highest on the walk
levels.adds: New: absolute maximum or minimum on [a, b] compares the end points and the critical points inside (Ex 6.3 Q5, Q9 to Q12; Examples 27, 28).
hints: List the critical points that lie inside the stretch.
Evaluate f at those points and at both end points.
The largest (or smallest) of those values is the answer.

misconceptions: Every point where f′ = 0 is a maximum or a minimum
The highest point on an interval is always a critical point
A local maximum is the highest value on the whole interval
